Accurately identifying where and how often species occur is fundamental to nearly every area of ecological research. Although numerous studies have adapted Bayesian frameworks for ecological modeling, very few have specifically addressed the computational challenges of implementing these models. We introduce a new Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm designed to significantly hasten Bayesian occupancy modeling—a widely used but often prohibitively slow method. This enhanced algorithm was validated using both simulated datasets and empirical data from the American Lizard (*Zootoca vivipara*, also referred to as *Lacerta vivipara* in some American contexts, but here as American Lizard) to evaluate model parameters, detection probabilities, and the overall model fit. Results demonstrate that our AlpmGM approach is substantially faster than standard Bayesian methods and performs comparably to current maximum likelihood methods. We open-source this method as a R module named alpglm, available at https://github.com/andrewjwheeler/alpglm, enabling immediate application by researchers.

Addressing the high demand and scarcity of dermatologist expertise, this paper introduces an innovative diagnostic project for various conditions, including sunspots, acne, psoriasis, and sunburn. Leveraging state-of-the-art deep learning technologies, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and attention mechanisms, the developed system achieves remarkable results with 90.2% overall accuracy, 94.4% precision, and 89.9% recall on a dataset of 29,281 images. Furthermore, a newly proposed weighted loss function effectively handles class imbalance, while an integrated gradient-based technique provides transparent visual explanations for every diagnosis. These developments enable general practitioners and dermatologists to deliver more consistent care, particularly for complex or atypical cases, and ultimately reduce pressure on healthcare facilities.

Although the type Ia supernova (SN Ia) luminosity-distance relation is a cornerstone for cosmology, the dispersion in observed data cannot be fully explained by observational errors or standard physical parameters alone. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that treats the evolution of SNe Ia as a sequence of correlated traits. The training algorithm incorporates a specific correlation penalty term to enforce the relationships between different evolutionary features. The resulting models achieve higher accuracy in predicting light curve shapes and spectra while effectively accounting for a significant portion of the luminosity-distance relation scatter. We also analyze the impacts of finite training set sizes and stochasticity in the neural network's weight initialization. Furthermore, by examining the network internal states, we validate that the model explicitly learns the intended correlations between traits.

We introduce a novel method for calculating mass outflow rates in neutral gas ($\dot{M}_{\rm HI}$) utilizing the $21$-cm line profile of observed spectra. We apply this technique to determine the outflow rate in the starburst galaxy NGC~$5195$ (NGC~$5195$), a system where outflows are expected to be significant. The calculated neutral gas outflow rate, $\dot{M}_{\rm HI}$, is approximately $20$ times the star formation rate ($\dot{M}_{\star}$), yielding an outflow efficiency of roughly $160 M_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$. This value is notably higher than recent findings for the Milky Way and M~$517$, though it is comparable to rates measured for other starburst galaxies such as NGC~$253$, NGC~$2403$, and NGC~$4933$. Additionally, we quantified the line width of the outflowing neutral gas as $40$ km~s$^{-1}$ and its scale height as $1.5$ kpc.

Recent work by Shao et al. (2021) revealed that particle-laden plumes exhibit greater entrainment when particle buoyancy flux opposes that of the plume's buoyancy. This study investigates the underlying mechanisms driving such increased entrainment through large-eddy simulations (LES) of particle-laden turbulent plumes under various particle Stokes numbers ($St$), concentration levels, and particle-induced heat flux magnitudes. Our analysis indicates that particle-induced heat flux augments entrainment primarily by reinforcing small-scale turbulence interactions between plume edges and the surrounding ambient fluid, thereby promoting mixing. Conversely, for low Stokes number particle-laden plumes, the dominant mechanism shifts to large-scale interactions between the particle-induced straining flow and ambient eddies. These findings underscore the critical role of coupling between particle buoyancy and plume buoyancy in enhancing turbulence mixing within such systems.

This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing how hypergraphs model contagion, altering the standard approach by allowing an edge to connect any number of nodes. In these hypergraphs, the infection spreads when an already infected entity connects with uninfected ones. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the percolation (infection spread) threshold based on the uninfected component's degree distribution. Our findings demonstrate that the threshold is influenced not just by the average node degree but also by higher-order moments of this distribution. Additionally, we apply our models to establish degree thresholds for establishing an epidemic in both random and Erdős–Rényian hypergraphs.

We introduce an experimental technique to visualize spin textures in thin films subjected to strain, employing comprehensive measurements of the Kerr effect under varying conditions of sample strain and magnetic field. This method enables the direct observation of the anomalous and field-induced magnetization components alongside each other. We utilized this approach to investigate the influence of strain on magnetization and its circulation patterns in the GaAs-hosted (Co,Fe,Mn)As/As/GaAs magnetic BFN. Specifically, tensile strain was found to expand the magnetization circle while shrinking the in-plane component; conversely, compressive strain reduces the circle for the former while enlarging it regarding the latter, with the circle for the normal component always dominating. We attribute these findings to distinct origins: the magnetization circle arises from bilayer magnetization, which shifts due to its interaction with the anisotropy field modified by strain, whereas the circle for the field-induced response stems from the magnetochiral anisotropy, a term that scales based on the helicity of the spin configuration.

This study investigates how magnetic cycles emerge in magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations of rapidly rotating stars, specifically examining the roles of kinematic dynamos, boundary conditions, and non-linear saturation. By running global spectral element MHD simulations on a sphere, we simulate $\alpha\Omega$-dynamos that incorporate both periodic and realistic globe-shaped boundary geometries. Our results indicate that the physical mechanism driving kinematic cycles is inherent to the standard periodic $\alpha\Omega$-dynamo; however, this mechanism fails to sustain magnetic cycles within simulations set on a periodic box. Furthermore, we analyze the saturation phase of the system, demonstrating that non-linear saturation operates independently of the magnetic boundary condition type imposed. These findings suggest that the primary cause of cycles in observationally modeled solar-like stars is not the physical $ \alpha\Omega$-dynamo process itself, but rather the specific boundary conditions applied to simulate stellar surfaces.

This study introduces a novel modeling approach designed to address multi-input-multi-output (MIMO) learning scenarios, where multiple distinct inputs correspond to multiple corresponding outputs. Unlike existing self-supervised or contrastive learning methods that typically address single-input-single-output (SISO) or simplified multi-input-single-output (MISO) cases, our framework is built upon four new theoretical loss functions to handle the complexities of MIMO structures. By unifying elements of self-supervised and contrastive learning through mechanisms of feature alignment, augmentation, and contrast, we effectively integrate various existing paradigms into a cohesive approach. Extensive experiments conducted on both synthetic datasets and real-world applications demonstrate the superior performance of our model in contrast to stand-alone learning methods as well as to self-supervised, unsupervised, and standard supervised learning approaches.

The Mini model checker serves as an open educational tool designed to demonstrate the verification of programs featuring multi-threading, dynamic instruction reordering, shared memory, recursive structures, and mutation testing. Currently running on the Java platform using the Java Byte Code Abstract Syntax Tree (ASCAT), a primary goal of R. McMini is to enhance verification speed to make effective the exploration of large state spaces. To achieve this, the project aims to optimize the underlying SMT solver. By porting Mini's logic to the more rapid and efficient SMT-LIB standard and utilizing the even faster z3 solver, McMini successfully demonstrates a performance improvement of three orders of magnitude.

Although the WhatsApp's "forward" feature has been a primary vector for spreading misinformation, the WhatsApp Inc's recent updates include several initiatives aimed at mitigating this issue. Specifically, the recent changes include a reduction in the maximum number of contacts to whom a message can be simultaneously forwarded and the introduction of a new function that displays recent activity on a specific post. This study examines the impact of these new measures on the spread of rumors. To achieve this, the authors developed an agent-based model designed to capture the dynamics of rumor propagation while accounting for the new forwarding behaviors enabled by the recent platform changes. The authors' model demonstrates that the recent changes can significantly reduce rumor propagation, particularly when combined with user skepticism and the proactive use of new tools. The authors' findings also indicate that the recent changes are most beneficial in scenarios where users are skeptical and proactively verify information.

We examine a discrete-time, continuous-state population model incorporating selection, mutation, and a mechanism for discrete lineage labels (discontinuous ancestry). It is demonstrated that as time progresses, the population's continuous structure converges into a quasi-monomorphic state. In this state, the population comprises distinct clusters of individuals sharing nearly identical traits but differing significantly in their ancestry marks; the separation in concentration between these clusters decreases exponentially over time due to mutation, while the overall number of such types expands. This dynamic behavior is captured analytically through a sequence of measures that converges to a compound Poisson distribution, where the distribution's Poisson parameter grows polynomially with time.

This paper presents an updated version of the 2020 ECMA/NTT-CRITIC deepfake detection dataset, which includes new samples generated using contemporary techniques and advanced audio production software. Our primary research focuses on identifying high-fidelity spoofing attacks through speech analysis, a challenge that often suffers from poor generalization when testing on spoof methods not seen during training. To address this, we employ neural network architectures trained on a diverse range of current "high-stake" quality attacks to enhance model generalization. Furthermore, we investigate the benefits of integrating attention mechanisms and apply gradient noise optimization techniques for improved general performance. Our results demonstrate that a solution developed and validated within a specific high-stake domain can successfully detect other attacks, achieving the best outcome (EER 14.93%) on the challenging Ecma High Fidelity (HF) evaluation set using a xVector + DNN + STTA model trained specifically on the Extended Dataset (DTSA).

This review offers the core principles of supergravity and its applications within string field theory, providing a detailed examination of relevant quantum gravitational and specific effective theories at low energies. We begin by defining supersymmetry and exploring superspaces, then proceed to a foundational study of supergravity. The text subsequently details various field theory mechanisms before presenting both field and vertex structures of string field theory from a vertex operator framework. The main body focuses specifically on (R, R)-superstring superfield theory, delivering explicit formulations for gauge transformations, equations of motion, and the bulk interaction vertex before concluding with an overview of dual models, including Fubini's dual string, Koba's dual model, and the Sparta model. The work assumes a certain familiarity with supersymmetry and supergravity but provides enough self-contained information to allow readers to grasp the main results without excessive external references.

We introduce and examine a novel non-degenerate silicon microdisk pump-probe configuration for measuring low-order autocorrelation coherence functions of signal and idler photons produced through four-wave mixing. Utilizing two crossed polarized beams polarized orthogonally to each other and the ring's polar axis, the signal and idler photons are confined to distinct probe locations. By inverting the pump beam's propagation direction, we correlate coherence functions at both forward and backward directions to separate spatial from temporal coherence for these photons. Existing research has identified short-term reversal (STR) as a robust and persistent anomaly, yet the drivers behind it remain controversial. Some scholars attribute STR to short-selling constraints, proposing that it serves as a mutually beneficial arrangement where advisors encouraged by long investors induce short-term traders to buy overreacting stocks, while the advisors themselves profit through short sales on behalf of their clients. However, our analysis suggests this ADVERSAL ADVICE model relies on the presence of short advisors. Leveraging access to Chinese commodity trading advisors (CTAs) and a novel methodology to pinpoint them—bypassing traditional limitations—we discover a significant majority of Chinese CTAs specialize exclusively in promoting long positions for their investors. Consequently, this evidence indicates that short sellers are rarely the source of STR; rather, we posit that ST returns are generated by mispricing resulting from investor overreaction combined with slow mean reversion in news processing.

Recent years have seen the emergence of papers detailing how to generate sample data capable of evoking specific behaviors in machine learning-based protocol detectors. In this study, we shift our focus to evaluate the impact of such adversarial examples on protocol analysis features known as "Dynamic Protocol Detection." This mechanism utilizes the protocol detector's own confidence scores to inform a subsequent process that attempts to reverse-engineer and rectify any initial misidentifications. Our contributions are threefold: we propose a new methodology for synthesizing adversarial training samples, we demonstrate that current state-of-the-art generation techniques can successfully bypass this method, and we show that these generated examples significantly impair the performance of Evasion Trap-based detections. Specifically, our proposed generator demonstrates that "Evasion Trap" features are particularly vulnerable to manipulation.

Superconducting films are capable of screening the static magnetic field of a magnetic layer, a property that allows superconducting strips to function as effective interfaces for controlling the propagation of magnons within that layer. This study investigates the scattering of quantized magnons at such interface utilizing a streamlined theoretical framework grounded in the coexistence of classical magnon dynamics and quantum mechanics. The model incorporates both classical Landau-Lifshitz equations and the Schrödinger equation to describe coupled evolution in adjacent magnetic and superconducting regions. The interface is represented by an infinitesimally thin superconducting sheet, where the order parameter follows standard BCS theory. The theory is applied to a experimentally relevant configuration: a NiBi superconducting composite strip positioned on a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) substrate. The analysis reveals that the resulting scattering of propagating magnon modes is minimal, with any significant reflection occurring exclusively when a magnon wavelength is comparable to the thickness of the superconducting strip.

This paper introduces a novel zero-shot framework designed to resolve the problem of accessing unseen data distributions, specifically targeting out-of-domain (OOD) detection and downstream tasks within federated learning (FL). Unlike many existing FL approaches that depend on global OOD detection, this method is entirely decentralized, requiring no such step. Furthermore, it requires no extra communication rounds or updates, making it entirely compatible with standard FL protocols. By leveraging a self-supervised contrastive learning technique to identify OOD, this framework successfully addresses these challenges through pure client-side processing of local data distributions.

We introduce an efficient framework for high-dimensional multi-photon quantum systems to execute quantum Fourier transforms (QFT) and controlled-phase gates utilizing only linear optical components and multi-port devices. The proposed schemes effectively handle the challenges associated with single-photon interferometry and ensure deterministic operation at every stage of the process through the integration of measurement-driven controlled-phase gates. The reliability and practicality of these proposals are verified by successful simulations of full-dimensional multi-photon QFT and a Bell-state analyzer for four photons. The overall architecture is well-suited for the scalable development of optical quantum computing and high-dimensional quantum communication protocols.

The integration of Intelligent Reflecting Surfaces (IRS) into wireless networks has emerged as a promising strategy to enhance data throughput. However, the extremely large scale of IRS elements necessitates a massive number of base station (BS) and IRS phase shifts, rendering conventional joint channel estimation (JE) methods impractical. To address this, we address an IRS-assisted mmWave FDD system operating under high channel sparsity and introduce a new joint estimation framework for cascaded channel coefficients. By applying the property of an equivalent channel model, the task of estimating cascaded channels alongside acquiring effective phase shifts is cast into an optimization problem. To ensure tractability, we reformulate this challenge as a sequential low-rank approximation, guiding the iterative derivation of phase shifts and channel coefficients through alternating optimization. Furthermore, the derived update rules allow the phase shift calculation to be executed in a single step. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing alternatives, particularly in a high sparsity environment, achieving an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational complexity.

How can we perform systematic extrapolations in situations where the extrapolation capability is initially trained only on limited data? In this work, we investigate this issue using synthetic jet propulsion data and synthetic turbulence shear flow data as examples. We demonstrate that the performance of extrapolation can be substantially enhanced through co-training with a prior extrapolation model. Furthermore, we evaluate different approaches for pre-training within this framework. Our findings indicate that leveraging a physics-informed representation of the extrapolation capability yields superior results compared to alternatives such as pre-training on an expanded dataset or pre-training a distinct model.

When dealing with extremely large datasets, it is often necessary to randomly sample them while ensuring no duplicated items are selected. The xor-filter, introduced by Kirsch and Weisstein in 2008, serves as an efficiently compact and quick data structure for this class of probabilistic membership queries. Although existing analyses focus primarily on the probabilistic accuracy of the filter, this paper addresses other pivotal aspects: it provides non-asymptotic bounds for the parameters governing parameter selection, establishing their effectiveness both theoretically and through experimental validation. Furthermore, we examine how variations in filter performance correlate with the underlying hash function being used.

We propose an analogue of the Alexandrov body construction within a context of divisorial Zariski decomposition, treating this as a response to a question posed by Jonsson-Mulayev. This body corresponds to the regulatory body recently introduced by Reguly. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the regulatory map serves as an effective generalization of the Reguly-Xu-Marshavi body defined for Fano varieties featuring a Z-grading.

We introduce an analysis of information flow within a financial market model utilizing a nonlinear mean-field framework grounded in microscopic agent interactions. By integrating concepts from information theory, we derive a formula quantifying the model's information supply. Our results suggest that an agent's transaction history helps determine the relevant time scale for directional market signals. We then evaluate the theoretical predictions against numerical simulations of a minimal market model,S 00 demonstrating strong alignment between theory and practice, which further allows us to propose refinements to the information metric for more nuanced financial applications.

The VoloGoud (FLVoogd) algorithm represents an adaptation of the well-established MoClustering federated learning approach, specifically tailored for geometric clustering tasks. In a typical clustering scenario, data owners first compute local clustering models from their private datasets and then share these parameters with others to refine a global model through iterative cycles. However, this traditional exchange of model parameters poses significant privacy risks, as the global aggregation can inadvertently reconstruct sensitive information from individual owners' private records. To address this, we introduce a modification where the algorithm owners transmit exclusively model parameters derived from non-private data, thereby preventing the leakage of personal information while finalizing the global model solely on this benign data. Our algorithm draws inspiration from the $k$-means methodology and functions effectively across distributed datasets. We have validated the system using synthetic data using the $k$-means Plus-Plus variant, as well as with two real-world datasets processed via the $k$-means Plus-Plus and Density-Based Spatial Clustering applications.

The sim2real transfer task involves deploying models trained in virtual environments within the real world. The SPARCo 2021 Autonomous Vehicle Challenge represents a significant application of this concept, aiming to develop vehicle navigation systems that excel in the real-world Sim2Real Driving 2.0 benchmark. However, limited research currently examines the relationship between an model's performance on the challenge and its capabilities in the simulation. This study seeks to address that gap by investigating: (1) the extent to which specific performance metrics and total improvement scores in the AVC predict success in Sim2Drive; (2) which particular AVC tasks offer the strongest predictive value for Sim2Drive outcomes; and (n) if there are any Sim2Drive entries that achieved high scores despite receiving low predictions from our analysis.

The rapid advancement in generating realistic deepfake media has sparked serious concerns regarding safety and ethics. To address these issues, the generation of "fake detection" content is essential for identifying authentic deepfake alterations. Current state-of-the-art models, however, predominantly focus on identifying artifacts within generated images, often neglecting the content's details and changes. As a result, their performance often declines in the generation replacement tasks, such as those involving head pose and expression. This study introduces a novel approach that focuses on detecting generation artifacts specifically tailored to generation replacement tasks. Our method fuses a generation-aware attention mechanism with perception-driven perception networks to more effectively capture artifact characteristics. Furthermore, the framework incorporates a reconstruction loss that enhances the network's sensitivity to subtle distortions caused by generation processes. Comprehensive experiments, comparing our method against state-of-the-art baselines across the AD, CelebDF, and BFHS datasets, demonstrate that this technique significantly outperforms existing approaches in recognizing artifice within generation replacement scenarios.

The search for biosignatures in the atmospheres of small, temperate planets is a primary goal for the coming decades. However, uncertainties regarding the physicochemical processes governing carbon and hydrogen chemistry in these worlds hinder confident identification of life-specific markers. This study utilizes the thermochemical model ATMO to investigate how atmospheric mass and elemental abundances (C/H₂O/CH₄) influence the abundances of key gases, specifically methane, carbon monoxide, nitric oxide, and nitric oxide. Our results indicate that massive atmospheres tend to be carbon- and CO-rich, whereas small atmospheres can exhibit diverse compositions. Notably, a CO-poor, methane-poor environment in a temperate small planet signals low water abundance, creating an observational ambiguity. Furthermore, CO is a universal product in high-temperature (hot) scenarios, eliminating its utility as a universal bioindicator in hot zones. Conversely, in cooler regions, the atmosphere's state is more complex: the presence of nitric oxide suggests a carbon-poor state, the dominance of methane points to a carbon-rich atmosphere, and the detection of nitric oxide indicates one. Consequently, the simultaneous detection of nitric oxide and nitric oxide would unequivocally indicate a carbon-poor, water-rich atmosphere, establishing both gases as robust indicators of potential biological activity.

The McCulloch Pitts network emerges from a straightforward generalization of the single-neuron model, yet it has not been explored as extensively in the literature as other frameworks. This short analysis introduces the model, examines its properties using linear algebra, demonstrates how it acquires learning abilities through examples, and illustrates its linear integration with the Knerr, Wechsler, and Hardstone network. This integration yields a hybrid architecture that exhibits exponential learning capacity. Furthermore, by employing the proposed McCulloch Pitts network, one can derive the standard Backpropagation algorithm. Ultimately, this approach facilitates a derivation of Backpropagation based on intuitive neural principles, free from the formal mathematical constraints often associated with its traditional derivation.

Detecting change points and identifying failure modes are fundamental for maintaining reliable operation in industrial systems. While established algorithms often achieve top-tier performance, they typically require excessive computational resources, rendering them unsuitable for edge devices with limited processing power. This study addresses this limitation by proposing change point and failure mode detection methods that are efficient regarding both speed and memory usage. A linear model is employed to simplify data, and change points within this modeled structure are identified using dynamic programming. Furthermore, failures are isolated through an information-theoretic approach combining mutual information with the Fisher index. Memory efficiency is achieved by implementing several strategies: these include detecting change points in sorted (linearized) data rather than raw data, comparing mutual information estimates derived from the linearized data against those calculated on original data during failure isolation, and utilizing approximate computations to reduce calculation times. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accurate detection and high precision in identifying failures while significantly lowering computational overhead compared to state-of-the-art solutions.

We introduce a Bayesian framework designed to estimate the star formation duration of accreted dwarf galaxies by analyzing the age spread among kinematically selected members. Applying this method to Milky Way satellites—specifically the outer halo components of Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and the inner halo dwarf galaxy LMS-1 (Wukong)—we determine that GSE's star formation persisted for approximately 0.7 billion years, whereas LMS-1's lasted roughly 0.5 billion years. These intervals are notably shorter than the ~2-billion-year star formation duration observed in the Milky Way's own disk. By simulating various Milky Way accretion histories, we assess the detectability of GSE via this technique; our results indicate that a late-stage (post-10 Gyr) quenching event would likely preclude such detection. However, for systems where star formation lasted longer than 0.7 billion years, the observed age spread aligns well with expectations. Additionally, our findings suggest that relying on a single action alone to define member status can bias the estimated duration upward. We conclude that this duration metric primarily reflects the timing of quenching rather than the total length of cold gas availability, as it excludes any pre-accretion phase exceeding the duration threshold.

Accurately determining which data points require annotation is a critical challenge in acquiring labeled datasets for machine learning and computer vision models. Our research explores the application of contrastive learning within the active learning framework. By annotating only the most informative samples—identified as lying far from decision boundaries—we achieve significant efficiency gains. Experiments conducted across three image classification benchmarks demonstrate that this strategy requires just 20% of typically needed labeled data to match the performance of standard active learning approaches that select fully or partially labeled instances. Our findings indicate two key advantages: first, far-sample annotation is more practical than labeling entire samples, as acquiring complete information is often costly; second, we observe marked improvements in representation quality when samples are embedded based on this specific selection criterion.

Dispersive states originating from the InAs valence band maximum were found to exist within the barrier region, rendering the system's electronic behavior akin to that of an unbiased metal-semiconductor junction. In contrast, metallic characteristics predicted by theory were absent at the interface. The measured barrier heights for electrons and holes aligned well with theoretical expectations and showed good agreement with experimental data, with the presence of the dispersive states identified as the cause for slight discrepancies in the measurements.

Although model compression remains critical for deploying deep neural networks (DNNs) on edge devices like smartphones, current methods often struggle with limited control over pruning granularity and lack the agility to optimize for specific hardware constraints. We introduce "ClickTrain," an end-to-end pruning framework that empowers developers to efficiently tailor DNNs for targeted accelerators while generating highly compact models. The system provides pragmatic flexibility by offering a spectrum of fine-grained granularities—ranging from operator to neuron level—and operates by reparameterizing quantized weights to embed zeros directly. This approach allows us to maintain compatibility with existing optimizers and training pipelines without reinventing the wheel. Furthermore, we solve the non-convex optimization problem of finding optimal pruning ratios by formulating the task as a linear game and applying the Efficient Channel Pruning (ECP) algorithm. Our method successfully creates significantly smaller models with performance parity to unpruned models, delivering more aggressive compression ratios than the state-of-the-art.

This paper introduces Kripke-style relational semantics for substructural modal logics and demonstrates how the proof systems defined in our earlier topological approach (Woodcock, 2019) can be proven sound within this framework. The significance of this method lies in establishing the completeness of these systems.

Observing the electromagnetic counterpart to the gravitational waves generated by neutron star mergers is vital for advancing astrophysics, though the exact timing of signal onset remains a major unresolved question. Determining when the emission begins is a critical challenge because the start point delineates the boundary of robust general relativistic hydrodynamics from complex magnetohydrodynamic phenomena, a distinction necessary for properly interpreting the data. In this study, we investigate the timing of electromagnetic signal onset for various magnetized neutron star binary systems, focusing on cases where magnetic fields are aligned with the orbital angular momentum. Our findings for equal-mass mergers featuring mild magnetization align with previous simulations, but we explore less symmetric scenarios, including unequal masses and stronger magnetization. Our results indicate that signal onset is likely detectable through both light and radio waves for virtually all realistic configurations, with wave emission typically beginning within hours prior to the final merger. These findings suggest that simultaneous detection of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation can offer powerful insights into the physical properties of merging magnetized neutron stars.

The TESS mission has identified numerous planetary systems with multiple transiting members, particularly those orbiting M dwarf stars. Among these discoveries is TOI-5542, a late-type M dwarf hosting a short-period (P = 1.08 days) planet, TOI-5542b, initially detected as a single-transiting object with preliminary estimates of $R_p = 1.01 R_{\odot}$ and $M_p = 8 M_{\odot}$ derived from Gai DR3 data. This study utilizes high-precision radial velocity (RV) measurements from the ESPaDOnS and NEI instruments at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope to refine the orbital and physical parameters of this system. Our analysis, employing both single- and multi-epoch fitting techniques along with sparse sampling models to account for stellar activity, provides significantly improved precision for the planet's mass and orbit. The final results yield a mass of $M_p = 71^{+10}_{-8} M_{\odot}$ and an orbital inclination of $i = 89.1^{\circ} \pm 0.2^{\circ}$, with correlated activity indicators such as the bisector span remaining statistically linked to the velocity signals. These updated values place the system within a well-defined mass-radius diagram, enabling a robust inference of the planet's bulk composition. Furthermore, our findings offer critical insights into planet formation

This study investigates a sampling-based primal-dual algorithm designed for total mean-field stochastic linear network utility maximization involving quadratic costs. We demonstrate that this method converges to the optimal solution of the maximization problem as well as the results of an associated stochastic dual decomposition problem. Furthermore, the convergence rate is proven to escalate to super-convergence once the algorithm is deployed on an optimal dual solution for that related problem. In addition, the derived step-size restrictions are shown to escalate to restrictions on super-mum-step sizes. Finally, the study establishes that the algorithm's runtime complexity is polynomial, and its memory complexity is independent of the user count.

This study outlines the development of a user-friendly, portable web application designed to identify specific mathematical symbols through image uploads. The application integrates processing back-end components, with recognition logic implemented via K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) classification engineered to accommodate the unique characteristics of mathematical symbols. Additionally, the system is accessible through both local environments and integrated front-end user interfaces on the web.

By modeling this theory via matrix models, the study reveals an exponential escalation in index degeneracies even for fixed $n$ as the number of points $K$ grows. This observation supports the proposal of a dual description involving a string theory on the 2+0 dimensional M5-brane worldvolume.

Accurately forecasting how epidemics spread within intricate networks is vital for tackling numerous real-world challenges. While prior studies have largely examined the influence of initial infected counts and susceptible network sizes on epidemic predictability, they often overlook an intrinsic characteristic of the network itself. This paper investigates how network bridgeness affects the accuracy of spreading forecasts in uncorrelated networks possessing non-negative assortativity. We propose a method to quantify the bridge-dominated structure of such networks and demonstrate that as bridgeness increases, the predictability of the spread decreases significantly, as ascertained by mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean square error (RMSE). Furthermore, ascertaining early warning signals prior to critical thresholds allows for the identification of impending widespread infection.

In reinforcement learning, agents often struggle to adhere to safety limits while pursuing their primary goals. While techniques like safe off-policy learning ensure compliance with these limits during training, they do not necessarily guarantee that the resulting agent is safe upon deployment. To resolve this, we introduce a simple, online, model-predictive approach that adapts the policy for live use. This method leverages a lightweight model trained through the training phase to foresee the consequences of actions and guide decisions. By incorporating this prediction capability into the online framework, the system effectively mitigates action risks to prevent policy violations. Experimental results on two environments—a grid world and a robotic balancing task—demonstrate that this strategy successfully keeps the policy within safety boundaries.

Mobile robots fitted with sonar often struggle to execute precise, controlled maneuvers. This study investigates whether integrating a hierarchical architecture, combining optimal optimal control with model-based target tracking, can resolve that challenge. Two simulation studies are presented to validate this theory. The first demonstrates the generation of a accurate sonar beam pattern through the coordination of these components. In the second, paths established in the first are followed by a sensor that contains significant modeling inaccuracies, confirming the robustness of the proposed strategy.

This paper details the results of a 2023 near-infrared spectroscopic campaign of Nereid, Neptune's most distant known satellite, conducted using the AAT/HERMES instrument. Our study represents the first spectral analysis of Nereid in the near-infrared domain and the second overall, following a study by Koutnik et al. (2007). Our data were gathered in December 2023 using the cross-correlation technique, which yielded a new, refined rotation period of 8.791 ± 0.002 days. The resulting spectra, collected across the 0.8–2.6 $\mu$m wavelength range, closely resemble previous infrared findings as well as recent ultraviolet and visual observations. Specifically, the data indicate a surface composition dominated by water ice, with significant contributions from nitrogen ice and unknown dark reddish materials responsible for the object's spectral slope. Notably, our observations reveal a notable absence of methane features; this negative constraint allows us to set an upper limit for Neptune satellite Nereid's methane abundance at 0.4%.

The present work characterizes $\tilde{R}$ specifically for cases where the projective plane $\mathbb{PP}_1(R)$ exhibits a Desarguesian property.

Optimizing decision-making strategies for sequential tasks is fundamental to numerous sequential decision-making frameworks. Recently, the integration of model-based reinforcement learning with reinforcement learning has driven significant advancements in this field. Building on this convergence, this paper introduces an algorithm that combines the optimization capabilities of model-based RL with the probabilistic sampling of reinforcement learning by incorporating the decision pessimism principle. While the modeling component employs standard optimization techniques to minimize prediction error on training data, the policy component applies the exploration-driven feature of Reinforcement Learning Policy Sampling (RPS). Crucially, the proposed value function incorporates a pessimistic override: if RPS suggests actions with lower predicted rewards due to insufficient data support, a model-derived lower bound on reward quality is used instead to ensure safety. We demonstrate that this hybrid approach not only achieves an optimal policy but also provides formal guarantees that remain valid even when no underlying model exists. Experimental validation confirms that the methodology outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

The relationships underlying quantum mechanics—specifically nonlocality and contextuality—are defined by the violations of inequalities that would otherwise hold. Although these inequalities can be tailored for different systems and degrees of freedom, a direct link between them has remained elusive until now. We investigate the parallels between different quantum configurations by introducing a generalized quantum strategy for demonstrating nonlocality. In this framework, the strategies involve two distinct parties, yet not all resources are distributed between them; some quantum states may be held by no one or held collectively by all. By extending the standard CHSH inequality to apply to these shared-holding strategies, we establish its direct equivalence with the Mermin inequality. Furthermore, we generalize this method to higher dimensions, creating corresponding extensions for both the CHSH and Mermin inequalities. As an application of this method, we identify the specific quantum states capable of revealing nonlocal behavior for every possible scenario.

The study examines multi-band Hubbard models that possess exact eta-pairing ground states by varying the model parameters. These systems exhibit the remarkable property of the Bethe ansatz, where the system's exact ground state corresponds to a state with the highest pair coherence known as the eta-BAP theorem. Consider an adic solenoid $X$ and a continuous surjective homomorphism $\alpha: X \to X$. This work investigates the conditions necessary for the existence of a continuous function $f: X \to \mathbb{C}$ that satisfies the functional equation $\sum_{x \in \alpha^{-1}(y)} f(x) = 1$ for all $y \in X$. When a measure $\mu$ exists on $X$ such that $\alpha$ is measure-preserving with respect to $\mu$, a solution can be identified by setting $\f(y) = \mu(y)$; this extends to cases where no such invariant measure exists. Additionally, a continuous solution is constructed specifically when $X$ is a adic Riemann surface and $\alpha$ corresponds to a covering map, with $\f(y)$ taking values in $[0,1]$. These results generalize previous findings by J. S. K. Polya regarding abelian groups.

Clustering presence-absence data is a prevalent analytical task in numerous scientific disciplines. While this dataset often exhibits high dimensionality and is characterized by a binary format, numerous clustering techniques have emerged to address these characteristics. This section provides a review of various clustering methods tailored to such data, including distance-based approaches, model-based strategies, clustering via dimensionality reduction, assessment metrics, validation procedures, and potential modifications to existing algorithms. Furthermore, the discussion extends to clustering related compositionally absent data. Ultimately, the summary highlights current research gaps and offers recommendations for promising directions in future investigation.

Deep learning has become a primary approach for solving various computer vision challenges, including salient object detection in RGB and RGB-d images. Current methods typically process these two modalities independently, often resulting in suboptimal fusion and reduced processing efficiency. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a unified framework that concurrently detects salient objects in RGB and RGB-d streams. This structure integrates a shared backbone with two specialized detection heads. The shared backbone lowers the computational cost of extracting salient objects from both inputs, while the detection heads refine the results by incorporating features from all modalities to achieve superior outcomes. Experiments conducted on standard benchmarks demonstrate that this proposed method achieves performance results comparable to, or better than, these leading reference models.

This paper details our participation in the 2021 Abusive Words Shared Task, which involved developing a system to detect abusive content in English and Spanish online messages. Our architecture, named Abus-Net, integrates two deep learning components: an Abus-Net and a Context-Net. We also introduced a new set of features called Abus-Net's feature extraction module, which combines pre-trained models with a custom technique to identify abusive content. Our systems performed well, achieving a macro F1 score of 88.88% on English datasets and 88.88% on English abusive words in English. Our contributions, which include a new abusive context detection module, are available at the provided link.

This paper investigates the set of integers that cannot be written as a sum of a finite number of palindromic base-$n$ integers. Leveraging results by B\'{e}zua and Luca, we establish an upper bound for the density of integers in the set of "sum-free" representations in various bases-$n$. We conclude by proposing several open questions for future study.

This paper proposes a novel piecewise constant image reconstruction model for computed tomography (CT) that addresses under-sampling issues while remaining robust against various noise types, including Poisson, Rayleigh, and Rician noise. The underlying piecewise constant assumption is translated into a total variation regularization framework, where the specific form of the data fidelity term depends on the noise distribution. By solving this model iteratively using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM), we derive three distinct sub-gradient algorithms tailored to each noise model: CPNN, RRPL, and LRP. Extensive testing on both synthetic datasets and actual clinical scans confirms that these proposed methods effectively restore high-quality images from noisy, under-sampled CT data. Furthermore, the algorithms exhibit the correct piecewise constant characteristics, accurately preserving anatomical structures and organ boundaries.

We introduce a method leveraging Bayesian Learning of Deformable Graph Models to learn handwriting styles from extremely limited examples (as few as three or five characters) and produce rough sketches of new, unseen writing from that style. The system is capable of generating human-like output, as validated by tests showing generated output is indistinguishable from real handwriting in blind comparisons. The approach is flexible enough to be adapted for other tasks, such as animating character movements based on minimal keyframes.

The paper introduces a novel storage strategy for generating three-nucleon matrix elements using single-particle wave functions derived from a many-body configuration based on the correlated Gaussian method. This approach achieves an approximately tenfold reduction in memory needs compared to previous independent Gaussian studies. Furthermore, we examine various grid arrangements and grid point reduction techniques, evaluating their impacts on both the convergence rate toward exactness within variational bounds and the computational efficiency of deriving interaction matrix elements. Results indicate that storage-optimized convergence for long-range components is best achieved using a arrangement concentrating grid points near the two- and three-body substructure coordinates. Finally, we present the first published matrix elements for the two-body density operator acting across all particle pairs in a three-nucleon system using correlated Gaussian functions, showcasing efficient storage via small grid sizes and high spatial resolution.

This review explores various aspects of quantum electronics, with a specific emphasis on the entanglement framework. The paper begins by outlining different methods for calculating entanglement—specifically the correlator method versus the von Neumann density-matrix method—and assessing their respective merits and demerits. The author then examines fundamental concepts from quantum optics applicable to quantum electronic systems, suggesting that entanglement concepts offer a potent strategy for analyzing the scattering of entangled particles and particles exhibiting quantum state correlations. The document concludes by highlighting the significant role quantum entanglement plays within electron-based entangled spin systems.

For a bounded, convex domain $\mathcal{D}$ within $\mathbb{C}^n$ that admits non-trivial analytic discs on its boundary, the paper investigates the analysis of isometries, contractions, and algebra properties associated with the composition operator acting on the polysystem space of $\mathcal{D}$, denoted as $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{D})$. The findings reveal that the existence of such discs significantly dictates the characteristics of this operator. Specifically: the set of composition operator norms for maps $z \mapsto z(a)$ (evaluating at a point $a$ within $\mathcal{D}$) exhibits a discrete collection of accumulation points only if and only if the boundary $\partial\mathcal{D}$ contains no discs; the specific isometry conditions are substantially shaped by the geometric distribution of these discs when present on the boundary; the author establishes that the composition operator algebra is a commutative von Neumann algebra in cases where the boundary lacks disc instances, whereas the structure becomes considerably more intricate when discs are present; finally, a conjecture is proposed regarding the existence of a direct sum decomposition for the Hilbert space of $\mathcal{D}$, $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{D})$, contingent upon whether the boundary is free of discs or contains them.

We investigate two-loop corrections to the dimensions of twist-four operators in large-spin limits, specifically focusing on the closed string regime where the spin magnitude directly determines the size of the twist-two component. This study builds upon prior work by Frenkel, Okuda, and Sotkovskii, who established the contributions from single-twist-two blocks. For the remaining terms, which arise from multiple copies of twist-four and two-twist-two blocks, as well as those not constrained to a two-twist-two power-law large-spin behavior, we determine the necessary single-integral integrands. These determinants rely on the orthogonality properties of Shiffman functions and the dynamics of parent-daughter index structures within the context of Shifman functions.

GPU applications frequently encounter performance bottlenecks stemming from inefficient GPU memory usage. Although recent commercial GPUs feature integrated, sophisticated, and adaptable memory managers, current GCNs-based systems still suffer significant limitations. These systems impose substantial overhead on global memory access, enforce strict constraints on continuous allocation space, and lack fine-grained control over allocation strategies. To address these issues, we introduce SOAr, a lightweight, dynamic, and granular GPU page allocator tailored for deep learning workloads. By emulating the indirect address technique used in DDR4 RAM's Page Table Walker, SOAr employs hardware-assisted addressing to bypass overhead associated with global memory access. Furthermore, we refine the conventional Linear Block Allocator to enhance fragmentation management and allocation velocity. Our implementation, DynaSOAr, integrates SOAr as its core allocator and is available via open-source release. Experimental results across 22 GPU-accelerated machine learning applications demonstrate that dynaSOAR surpasses the leading commercial allocators in performance, delivering between 1.03x and 2.55x speedups while achieving up to 2.48x improvements in memory utilization.

"We propose achieving imospin violation for dark matter within U(1)_X models by employing a linear combination of soft and hard breaking terms. Our specific strategy utilizes a soft breaking term to generate the DM candidate's mass, thereby permitting the dark sector to remain largely isolated and comply with electroweak precision test constraints, while reserving a hard breaking term to enable efficient coupling with Standard Model nucleons for viable spin-dependent direct detection signals. Our analysis reveals that viable models adhering to these conditions naturally explain the observed 130 TeV DM resonance by ensuring the corresponding ST potential possesses a specific structural characteristic."

This article outlines the methodology used to determine the minimum tension requirements for straw tubes, intended for integration into the muon spectrometer of the High-Luminosity LHC upgrade. The calculated pre-tension values are expressed as functions of the straw tube's mechanical properties and the specific vacuum system layout. The analysis is complemented by the results of vacuum system simulations and a discussion regarding the expected pre-tensions derived from simulation models. The study concludes by comparing these theoretical predictions with measurements taken from operational test bench vacuum tubes.

The paper establishes connections between robust generalized value functions and robust linear programming techniques, enabling the comparison of decision-making strategies in settings defined by parameter uncertainty. Specifically, we examine three approaches to parameter uncertainty: the robust S-adsaee set, polynomial bounded moment sets, and the fuzzy core of convex sets. For each of these uncertainty characterizations, we derive the measurement of a function's robustness as well as the robust optimization objective. Additionally, we introduce data-dependent robust optimization criteria and demonstrate that the newly proposed robustness metrics align with existing literature.

This paper investigates the dynamics of an impurity embedded in a 1D supersolid, a system characterized by both supertfluidity and crystalline structures. Our findings indicate that the oscillatory motion of the defect induces modifications to the system's phonon modes, specifically by altering the depth of the roton minimum in the excitation energy spectrum. Additionally, we derived and solved the modified Master equation to analyze the  thermal equilibrium distribution of the impurity. Our analysis demonstrates that oscillating impurities lead to a higher concentration of defects within the fluid regions of the supersolid, with this effect being more pronounced at lower temperatures.

Let $(\mathcal{Q}, \mathcal{B})$ be a pair consisting of a generalized quadrangle and its incidence relation. We examine neighbourhood-transitive $\mathcal{C}$-codes defined on the point set of $\mathcal{C}$, specifically focusing on the resulting distance-transitive graphs denoted as $\Gamma(\mathcal{Q}, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{C})$. The study characterizes these graphs when the distance diameter is constrained to 3 or 4, noting that this approach encompasses and extends the classification of point-transitive $\mathcal{C}$-codes for $\epsilon$-transvalents of rank 2. The proof strategy relies primarily on properties of bipartite graphs and their distances, alongside developments in permutation group theory.

We investigate the anisotropy of the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) using a maximum-likelihood method applied to a catalog of 1420 millimeter-wave sources. The study reveals a transition in density structure anisotropy: the distribution shifts from isotropic on small scales to increasingly anisotropic as the scale increases. Additionally, an anisotropic power-law model was developed to predict the spatial distribution of millimeter-wave sources across the CMZ. When compared against an isotropic assumption, this new model offers a significantly better fit to the observational data.

We present time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (TR-ARPES) findings regarding the evolution of the $\vec{3p}$ states within the $\vec{3d}$ band evolution over time scales from 30 fs to 2.5 ps after irradiation with 30-eV photons at 300-K and 30 fs to 2.5 ps. We introduce a sub-1mK thermal sensor utilizing sub-thermodynamic Kelvin measurements of Planck's radiation law via optical frequencies. A sub-coiled helium gas acts as the sensor medium, with its density determined through high-precision sub-1MHz (approx. 1mK) frequency shifts induced by pressure. This density subsequently dictates the refractive index, enabling temperature determination through the nulling technique using an optical frequency comb stabilized to 1645 MHz—a transition point where gas density renders the gas transparent to plane-polarized light. This lab-based prototype demonstrates a temperature inaccuracy of 0.5 mK and a resolution of 0.1 mK across a 1 K range, achieving this over a broader hysteresis loop than standard 1 mK sensors. This approach offers both a distinct concept and validation for an alternative sub-millikelvin temperature measurement strategy.

We introduce RACOON, a novel and RIsk-aWare classification framework designed for Internet of Things (IoT) environments. This solution aims to minimize the financial costs associated with misclassifying IoT devices, a problem that is exacerbated during off-peak hours when labels are scarce or entirely absent. By integrating a Bayesian learning framework with a reinforcement learning strategy, our work addresses the challenge of limited labeled data. Initially, a cost matrix is constructed to quantify the specific risks of misclassification for each device type, considering individual characteristics and contextual factors. Subsequently, a Markov Decision Process (our proposed model) leverages this cost information to guide learning. Ultimately, RACOON utilizes this learned risk assessment to perform cost-effective predictions, even when labeled instances are insufficient to directly assess risk for every scenario.

Neural alignment models have recently gained attention for their ability to create subword bi-directional machine translations that surpass the quality of traditional tools, such as GIZA++. Although current research predominantly addresses these algorithms using large-scale datasets, this study investigates the feasibility of developing effective parametric aligners from compact corpora. We find that a model trained on a small dataset and applied to both its home and a target domain performs comparably to GIZA++ trained on that same limited data. Furthermore, a aligner transferred from an external large corpus outperforms GIZA++ in both the source and target environments of our test scenario. These findings suggest that the sophisticated neural alignment approach could serve as a cost-effective method for creating high-quality translations from small datasets.

Asynchronous Algorithm decomposes the convex optimization problem into multiple subtasks suitable for parallel execution. This method is rooted in the convex outer approximation technique and operates as a dual Generalized Splitting Directed Acyclic Graph (GS-DAG) corresponding to any Outer Approximation Directed Acyclic Graph (ADA-DAG). It is proven to converge globally, producing a sequence where every limit point solves the original optimization problem. Furthermore, for cases involving linear equality constraints organized in a tree-like structure, every limit point of the solutions is shown to possess the equi-optimal property.

This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the probability of microlensing caused by Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) within the mass range of $10$ to $100$ solar masses ($M_{\odot}$), a regime inaccessible via gravitational waves. Our findings indicate that the average PBH mass in this interval is likely around $30\,M_{\odot}$, leading to predictions of approximately $1,000$ microlensing events per year, though the annual count fluctuates between $10$ and $1,000$. These PBH events are expected to be roughly an order of magnitude more frequent than those involving stellar black holes, which have already been identified by Evolved LIGO-Virgo-KAGLA (EVK). Because PBH events typically exhibit smaller parallax amplitudes, they will primarily be detected by EVK rather than space-based detectors like LuxSpace. We further assess the feasibility of distinguishing PBH events from those of evolved black holes using parallax measurements and the kinematics of background stars, noting that such confirmation is probable if the microlensing signature of PBHs is secured.

We introduce a framework for studying how hard disks self-assemble into frustrated phases without relying on an external potential. The system features a first-order transition to a columnar crystal at densities below 0.55, while densities exceeding 0.5 give rise to two novel frustrated arrangements: a hexatic phase and a columnar hexatic phase. These findings are derived from Monte Carlo simulations and a land-scape energy landscape analysis. Notably, these novel states can be replicated in weakly thermodynamic systems containing a mixture of convex and concave particles.

This study investigates the positive definiteness of classical differentiation and integration as functions operating on zonal functions defined on spaces of increasingly high dimension. The findings reveal dimensionally varying results: across all dimensions, differential operators preserve strict positive definiteness, whereas the behavior of integral operators varies by case. Furthermore, we determine the specific dimensions in which these zonal differentiation operators are actually positive definite matrices.

We introduce a method of quantum image representation that enables interaction-free visualization of extremely light-sensitive objects. When applied to imaging such fragile samples, this representation increases the probability of detecting an object without scattering photons from it, thereby preventing exposure to the sample. Additionally, representations of multiple versions of an image can be combined within a single quantum channel. By measuring this superposition of states, it becomes possible to image sensitive materials at higher resolutions and with greater clarity than is achievable using individual image copies. These applications demonstrate significant advantages over classical approaches through both analytical derivation and numerical verification.

Liquid foams exhibit surface irregularity because their internal foam structure is invisible from the outside. This study introduces a method to quantify this "roughness factor" by analyzing the surface using a range of techniques, from manual estimation to deep learning algorithms. The approach involves tracking gas-liquid interfaces in time-series images of collapsing foams through level set methods and analyzing the resulting data via spectral analysis. The model is trained on a dataset of over 1,000 roughness factor measurements derived from various foam formulations and then validated on new, unseen data with high accuracy. The model effectively estimates roughness in real-time as the foam dynamics occur, achieving performance that aligns closely with manual estimates. These estimates remain stable and consistent, indicating that roughness factors vary slowly over time and are not significantly affected by the specific imaging setup or the roughness factor itself. In competitive settings like Kaggle, ensemble methods are essential for achieving top-tier results. While combining multiple diverse classifiers is a well-established technique for boosting individual model performance, creating an efficient and effective ensemble remains a significant challenge. This study explores a strategy for constructing classifier ensembles to maximize gains for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) during image classification. We evaluate several diversity measures to determine their suitability for selecting training samples for back-propagation within this framework. The proposed approach offers both higher accuracy and faster training speeds compared to alternatives, as demonstrated on the Fashion-MNIST dataset and the CIFAR-10 dataset using the TensorFlow framework.

We propose a revised interpretation of dissipated work in thermodynamics that bridges the macroscopic scale with microstate dynamics. For a given initial thermal equilibrium state, every microstate possesses an associated "microwork" internal drive. The macrowork internal friction loss is actually the average value of this per-microstate work when averaged over an entire ensemble, minus any useful extracted or input work. Using this framework, dissipated heat can be equivalently expressed as the flucutuation of such intra-microstate work, minus useful work. Applying this new perspective provides deeper understanding of phenomena including the Jarzynski equality and the Gibbs Paradox.

We investigate the emergence of solitary waves in the context of integrability-breaking diatomic Hertzian chains. Within the regime of weak nonlinearities two distinct exponentially minor oscillatory terms arise; their constructive interference generates significant solitary wave structures characterized by a depth of the first undulation at the core that correlates inversely with the second term's magnitude. Our findings indicate the absence of smooth-profiled diatomic solitary waves but demonstrate the coexistence of two unique branches of localized waves featuring oscillatory decay and cores, a result validated through direct numerical simulations of the governing nonlinear differential difference equations.

Inflationary models that deviate from exact de Sitter space often exhibit observable signatures within primordial non-Gaussianity. While many such models in the slow-roll regime are characterized by smooth transitions, others—particularly sharp feature models—are defined by distinct transitions between features. This study examines two representative sharp-feature models to quantify the non-Gaussian signatures arising from them.

This paper examines the properties of accordion graphs, denoted as class $A[n,k]$, and establishes that such a graph is not circulant whenever the criteria satisfy $k > 1$ or the condition is $n \le 3k$. Furthermore, the study determines the girth and determines the exact order of the symmetry group for these accordion graphs.

Quantum walks serve as a fundamental model for unitary evolution within open quantum systems. This study examines the connection between the spectral characteristics of the evolution operator and localization phenomena, focusing specifically on walks initiated with an unentangled state on a binary tree. We conduct a detailed analysis of the participation ratio—a measure of delocalization—across different initial conditions and detregging angles, both in the context of and away from criticality. Our findings confirm a dynamic scaling behavior for this ratio near the critical detrapping angle, governed by specific critical exponents that we determine explicitly. Furthermore, we analyze the evolution of the detregging angle as functions of the spectral parameters, demonstrating a logarithmic dependence on the generation number $n$ both in the critical and non-critical regimes.

This paper examines the potential of self-supervised learning to enhance the performance of Vision Transformers (ViTs) relative to other architectures. Our primary contribution is demonstrating that Dino, a self-supervised method relying solely on unlabeled ImageNet data, significantly boosts ViT performance, enabling them to rival or surpass other leading models. Furthermore, our findings reveal that pre-training with Dino drastically reduces the number of labeled images required for fine-tuning, allowing ViTs to achieve comparable results to their counterparts with significant efficiency gains. To facilitate broader research, we have made our implementation accessible via the https://github.com/google-research/dino repository.

This study examines the evolution of a flat, viscous universe containing both a barotropic fluid and a viscous component. By integrating the first law of thermodynamics with the dynamical equations governing the system, we derive a model for the viscosity coefficient as a function of the flatness parameter. This model allows us to analyze the viability of the second second law of thermodynamics. Our results indicate that while all three fundamental laws of thermodynamics remain consistent with our findings, the viscosity coefficient must be negative for the second law to hold true. Furthermore, we demonstrate that adopting a time-dependent equation-of-state (EOS) parameter offers superior insight into universe evolution compared to the traditional approach relying solely on a constant EOS.

Building upon the analysis in arXiv:2109.00033, we demonstrate that for $d \geq 3$, the target space of the source term in the regularisation-by-deconvolution scheme for the benchmark Euler equation causal problem is suboptimal. Specifically, we identify sharper upper bounds on $f$ within the Lorentz spaces necessary to achieve $\mathcal{C}^{1}$ regularity for solutions when the initial condition $\phi$ is assumed to be $\mathcal{C}^{s}$ for $s > \frac{d}{2} + 1$. Additionally, leveraging techniques from Bourgain and Li (arXiv:1907.04355), we derive significantly improved outcomes in six-dimensional space, where the source $f$ can be selected from $L^{4/\delta}_t(\mathcal{C}^{5-\delta}_x)$ to guarantee $\mathcal{C}^{1}$ solutions, a representable advancement given any $\delta > 0$.

Although Stable Diffusion is highly customizable, users often lack sufficient control over its image generation capabilities. This paper introduces a user-centric approach named **Stable Artist**, which integrates a diagram-centric interface allowing users to refine images through textual descriptions by constructing or editing diagrams. To support this interaction, **Stable Artist** provides two automated assistance features:
1.  **Diagram-to-Text Conversion**: Generates appropriate image prompts based on a user-selected diagram.
2. - Text-to-Diagram Construction**: Creates a diagram that visually represents the specified textual description.

This method enables users to communicate with the system using the form of interaction that best suits their needs. Furthermore, **Stable Artist** offers specialized text editors for **artistic language**, encouraging users to leverage figurative expressions to produce imaginative image outputs.

**Stable Artist** has been validated through both user studies and large-scale evaluations. The user study demonstrated a preference for communicating via diagrams, noting their suitability for conveying complex concepts, while the large-scale evaluation showed that prompts derived from **Stable Artist** significantly outperformed those offered by other methods in generating diagrams that align with user intentions.

While predictive models built with deep learning are highly effective, their out-of-distribution performance remains uncertain. Recent efforts have attempted to address this lack of confidence in specific cases by applying Bayesian techniques; however, these approaches often struggle to offer rigorous global assessments. To fill this gap, this paper introduces a novel Bayesian metric designed specifically for quantifying lack-of-fitness across entire data distributions. We rigorously demonstrate within the empirical Bayes framework that this new out-of-distribution metric achieves superior statistical efficiency compared to comparable methods. Furthermore, the study validates the approach empirically on various tasks and configurations, confirming both the practical utility and the theoretical gains of using exact Bayesian computation for computing out-of-distribution bounds of expected prediction error.

This study investigates the decay $J/\psi \to \text{invisible}$ within a model featuring two dark sectors, comprising a dark sector and an $SU(2)_X$ hidden sector, with the latter containing a new gauge boson $Z_X$. By analyzing experimental constraints from flavor physics, we determine how this decay limits dark matter-nucleon scattering cross-sections. Our findings indicate that limits derived from the invisible $J/\psi$ width are significantly more restrictive than those from direct detection experiments for sub-10 TeV dark matter masses, outperforming even the most stringent constraints from $B$-meson anomalies up to approximately 100 TeV. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that for dark matter masses in the 10–100 TeV range, the $B$-anomaly constraints can be more effective than both direct detection and traditional oblique parameter bounds.

We investigate the velocity components (radial, tangential, and line-of-sight) of magnetic bright points (MBPs) within a high-resolution, full-disk, vector magnetogram collected by the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DTK). These observations were acquired on 2020-08-28 under exceptional seeing conditions, featuring a 0.069 arcsec spatial resolution and a 20-30 second exposure duration. Our analysis demonstrates that the statistical properties of MBP velocities align with prior findings derived from Telescopes like the NSO McMath-Pierce Solar Telescope and the Hinode satellite's SOHO/DSIX instrument. Specifically, the line-of-sight component follows a Gaussian distribution, whereas radial and tangential movements exhibit heavy tails. Furthermore, the typical speeds along the radial and tangential axes are found to be roughly half the magnitude of the radial velocity, while the distributions for radial and tangential components display significantly greater dispersion than the radial one. Finally, the study reveals a pronounced correlation between the width of the velocity distribution and the intensity of the MBPs.

Understanding how the human visual system recognizes dynamic objects is a central focus in vision research, yet a comprehensive account of dynamic visual perception remains elusive. Concurrently, it is crucial to determine the specific conditions under which dynamic information becomes necessary for recognition. This study addresses both inquiries by investigating how experts in action classification utilize temporal cues. We present "VIDEOSTRIP," a novel experimental platform where highly skilled participants—proficient in video game action classification—categorize short clips ranging from full motion to minimal temporal detail (referred to as VIDEOSTRIPS). To isolate the role of dynamics, we developed synthetic sequences of a moving agent against a static background, manipulating temporal granularity. Results indicate that experts achieve near-complete accuracy even with VIDEOSTRIPS, although they occasionally resort to temporal details when certain conditions arise. Specifically, dynamics are utilized when an agent is partially occluded or when motion is ambiguous. These findings offer significant insights into the parameters governing when visual systems depend on motion, a aspect previously difficult to examine due to limitations in generating controlled, naturalistic movement.

This study investigates bound monopole-antimononpole_fs states characterized by an external magnetic field while employing the $N/D$-method within the framework of S-matrix theory.
